main.text: [III, 205] Chapter 12. [col. 416]
It is proved that שפיפון sephiphon, Gen. XLIX, 17, is the cerastes and the haemorrhous.

At Gen. XLIX, 17, I cannot at all understand why the Greeks rendered שפיפון sephiphon as ἐγκαθήμενον [enkathēmenon], and the Samaritans as ࠊࠌࠉࠍ · lying in ambush. But I know that others hold, much more correctly, that שפיפון is a kind of serpent. For this is openly proclaimed by the words of Jacob, which run thus: DAN shall be a serpent by the way, a שפיפון sephiphon by the path, that bites the horse's heels, so that his rider falls backward. Thus it is quite certain that the sesiphon is a serpent. Only the species is in doubt. The Hebrews, indeed, concern themselves solely with the origin of the word. Aben Ezra derives it from the verb שוף, to bruise, because it was said to the serpent in Gen. III, 15. אתה תשופנו עקב, You shall bruise his heel. Kimchi derives it from the verb שפה, which also has the meaning to bruise in Iob. XXXIII, 21. So שפיפון would be formed from שפה with the second radical doubled, as הגיגי from הגה. But Selomo and Pomarius prefer to derive it from נשף, to blow, or to hiss. This is what the Hebrews say on the origin of the word; on its proper meaning, οὐδὲ γρύ [oude gry]. If you consult others, however, their very diversity will leave you doubtful and uncertain. Jonathan explains it as רישי חיוין, the chief of serpents; Onkelos as פתנה, an asp; the Jerusalem Targum and the Syriac as ܡܥܪܘܢܐ, a basilisk; both Arabic versions as معرون [maʿrūn], explaining the unknown by the more unknown; Jerome as cerastes; Junius as acontias; Schindler, under ארח, as viper; Castalio and the Italian, French and English versions as snake.

In this darkness we borrow some light from the Arabs, among whom سف sipphon, or supphon, is a serpent marked with white and black. Alcamus: السف الارقم من الحيات [al-siff al-arqam min al-ḥayyāt], Sipphon (or supphon) is, among serpents, the one called [col. 417] arkamo (variegated). And elsewhere: الارقم اخبث الحيات واطلبها للناس او ما فيه سواد وبياض [al-arqam akhbath al-ḥayyāt wa-aṭlabuhā li-l-nās aw mā fīhi sawād wa-bayāḍ], Arkamo, the most pernicious of serpents and the most hostile to man; or one that is partly black, partly white. Hence there is a weighty conjecture that the sipphon is the haemorrhous and haemorrhois, of which Aëtius says: These animals are sandy in colour, etc. But over the body they are variegated with black and white marks. Likewise Avicenna ^{a)}: ذكرت القدما ان هاتين الحيتين رمليتا الابدان وعلي ابدانها نقط سود وبيض [dhakarat al-qudamā an hātayn al-ḥayyatayn ramliyyatā al-abdān wa-ʿalī abdānihā nuqaṭ sūd wa-bīḍ] The ancients report that these serpents have sandy bodies, and that these are sprinkled with [III, 206] black and white spots. So if שפיפון sephiphon is explained from Arabic usage, it will seem to be the haemorrhois, a species of viper whose bite draws out blood, so that whatever life there is is summoned out through the blood, as we read in Solinus.

Yet the Vulgate version, which renders it cerastes, greatly appeals to me, because the nature of the cerastes seems plainly expressed in Jacob's words, "Dan shall be a serpent by the way, שפיפון עלי ארח, a sephiphon by the path"; or, as others render it, on the wheel-track. For that is where the cerastes lurks, as Nicander says in the Theriaca, line 262.
— — — ἐν δ᾽ ἀμάθοισιν Ἠ καὶ ἁματροχιῇσι παρὰ στίβον· — — [en d᾽ amathoisin ē kai hamatrochiēsi para stibon]

In the sand, or even in the wheel-ruts beside the road, so as to lie in wait for travellers from there. And Jacob adds that the sephiphon bites the horse's heels so that the rider falls backward, namely when the horse stumbles as the poison begins to creep into its hocks. For the same Nicander relates that the force of the evil shows itself chiefly in the hollows of the knees and in the groin:

Διπλοῖς δ᾽ ἐν βουβῶσιν, καὶ ἰγνύσιν ἀσκελὲς αὐτὸς Μόχθος ἐπιτρέφεται· — — — [Diplois d᾽ en boubōsin, kai ignysin askeles autos Mochthos epitrephetai] Soon heavy suffering afflicts the groin, and pain sharply presses both knee-hollows. — — —

And this bite is deadly not only to men but also to beasts. For Callias in Aelian, book 16, chapter 28, says: Τοὺς κεράστας ὄφεις δεινοὺς εἶναι τὸ δῆγμα, ἀναιρεῖν γὰρ τὰ ζῶα ἄλογα, καὶ ἀνθρώπους· [Tous kerastas opheis deinous einai to dēgma, anairein gar ta zōa aloga, kai anthrōpous] The cerastes serpents are dangerous in their bite, and kill both beasts and men. What is most serious is that the ambush of the cerastes is not easily avoided: since it is the colour of the sand, it is trodden on by the unwary, whom it bites in return. Diodorus, book 3 ^{b)}: Τὴν δὲ χρόαν ἄμμῳ παραπλησίαν ἔχουσι· διόπερ ἐξωμοιωμένων αὐτῶν κατὰ τὴν πρόσοψιν τοῖς ὑποκειμένοις ἐδάφεσι, ὀλίγοι μὲν ἐπιγινώσκουσιν· οἱ πολλοὶ δ᾽ ἀγνοοῦντες πατοῦσι, καὶ κινδύνοις περιπίπτουσιν ἀπροσδοκήτοις. [Tēn de chroan ammō paraplēsian echousi; dioper exōmoiōmenōn autōn kata tēn prosopsin tois hypokeimenois edaphesi, oligoi men epiginōskousin; hoi polloi d᾽ agnoountes patousi, kai kindynois peripiptousin aprosdokētois.] They resemble sand in colour; therefore, since they are like the ground beneath them in colour, few recognize them, and most tread on them unawares and so fall into unforeseen dangers. Hence it came about that these serpents once entirely depopulated a part of Ethiopia bordering on Egypt, as Diodorus relates in the same place.

Now, if the matter is decided by authority, the Vulgate agrees with both Arabic versions, in which معرون [maʿrūn] is the cerastes, like Avicenna's مقرنة [muqarrana]. In those languages Koph and Ajin are not rarely interchanged. Hence among the Chaldeans and Syrians earth is called ܐܪܥܐ [III, 207] and ܐܬܢܢ; to smoke, ܩܘܦܣ and ܟܦܣ; cold, ܩܘܦܣܐ and ܟܦܣܐ. And in Jonathan רקם is the same place that the Hebrews call עצמון, Num. XXXIV, 4. In the same way among the Arabs horn is both عرن [ʿarn] and قرن [qarn]. Giggeius, from Alcamus: عران البقر [ʿirān al-baqar] [col. 418] the horns of oxen, عرنة [ʿirna] the root of the horns, عرون [ʿarūn] the slug, the snail, namely ^{c)} because of the two little horns with which it feels its way, since it lacks the use of eyes. By the same reasoning the cerastes is called both مقرن [muqarran] and معرون [maʿrūn], that is, horned, or having little horns like those of a snail ^{(1)}. Aelian: Ὑπὲρ τοῦ μετώπου κέρατα ἔχει δύο, καὶ ἔοικε τοῖς κοχλίου τὰ κέρατα, οὐ μέν ἐστι ὡς ἐκεῖνα ἁπαλά· [Hyper tou metōpou kerata echei dyo, kai eoike tois kochliou ta kerata, ou men esti hōs ekeina hapala] Above its forehead it has two horns, similar to the horns of a snail, though not equally soft. Pliny, however, in book 11, chapter 37, says that the horns of both the cerastes and the snail are corporeal, that is, fleshy. Accordingly Belon does not call them horns, but small protuberances like grains of barley, which resemble little horns ^{(2)}. Hence it is evident that those ^{d)} are not a little mistaken who write that knife handles for the tables of emperors are made from the horns of cerastes, because they betray poison placed nearby by sweating. For who would make knife handles out of so tiny a horn, and a soft one at that? Not to mention that it is not reasonable that the little horns of a poisonous animal should have an ἀλεξιφάρμακος [alexipharmakos] power. But the barbarous writers wrongly attribute to the horns of the cerastes what they had read somewhere about the horn of the كركدان [karkadān] carcaddan, or monoceros. Of it, namely, the Nubian Geographer, Clim. 1, section 8: ملوك الهند [III, 208] تصنع من قرن هذه الذابة انصبة السكاكين للموايد فانا وضع الطعام بين ايديهم وكان فيه سم عرق ذلك النصاب فيعلم بذلك ان الطعام مسموم [mulūk al-hind taṣnaʿ min qarn hādhihi al-dhāba anṣibat al-sakākīn lil-mawāyid fa-anā wuḍiʿa al-ṭaʿām bayna aydīhim wa-kāna fīhi samm ʿariqa dhālika al-niṣāb fa-yuʿlam bi-dhālika anna al-ṭaʿām masmūm] The kings of India have knife handles made for themselves from the horn of this animal for use at table. And when food is set before them, if it is poisoned, those handles become moist with sweat. From this it is detected that the food is infected with poison. Did Epiphanius have something of this kind in mind when, writing against the Pneumatomachi, he mentions κεράστου δεινοῦ μονοκέρωτος [kerastou deinou monokerōtos], of the dread one-horned cerastes? I do not think so; rather, in his opinion the serpent cerastes is one-horned. For he says the same about the heresy of the Basilidians: Ὡς κεράστου τρόπον ἐν ἄμμῳ κεχωσμένη, διὰ δὲ τοῦ κέρατος ἐν ἀέρι προκύπτουσα, καὶ τὸν ὄλεθρον τοῖς περιτυγχάνουσιν αὐτὴν ἐργαζομένη· [Hōs kerastou tropon en ammō kechōsmenē, dia de tou keratos en aeri prokyptousa, kai ton olethron tois peritynchanousin autēn ergazomenē] Buried in the sand like the cerastes, with its horn thrust up into the air, deadly to those who come upon it.

To return to the matter: it has so far remained uncertain whether the sephiphon is the cerastes or the haemorrhous, since much favors each interpretation. We have said that Jerome and both Arabic versions render it cerastes, and that this interpretation agrees excellently with the words of the Patriarch. Yet the sipphon, a similar word, is so described by the Arabs that it seems rather to be the haemorrhous. What if we say that sephiphon is a name common to both? That certainly seems to be so. And hardly anyone will call this into doubt who knows how similar the cerastes and the haemorrhous are. Each is a species of viper. Both are sand-colored, but the haemorrhous is spotted. Both are of the same size. Avicenna on the haemorrhous and the haemorrhois: واطوالها اطوال المقرنه [wa-aṭwāluhā aṭwāl al-muqarrana] Their length is the same as that of the cerastes. Nor does the haemorrhous lack horns, as Aelian testifies in book 15, chapter 13: Φρίττει δὲ τὴν κεφαλὴν οἱονεὶ κέρασί τισιν· [Phrittei de tēn kephalēn hoionei kerasi tisin] Its head bristles as if with certain horns. And long before, Nicander:
Τοῦ μὲν ὑπὲρ νιφόεντα κεράατα δοιὰ μετώπῳ [col. 419] Ἔγκειται· — — — — [Tou men hyper niphoenta keraata doia metōpō enkeitai] Above its forehead two horns are seen, whiter than snow. — — — — —

Thus the haemorrhous is a species of cerastes, or horned serpent. This is especially notable: whereas the other serpents creep straight forward, the cerastes and the haemorrhous alone move with an uncertain and wavering gait, staggering to either side, drunk, so to speak, or like one who limps. Hence Aëtius on the cerastes: It creeps obliquely, not straight. And Isidore: It is more sinuous than other serpents. And Aelian on the haemorrhous too: Λοξὸν δὲ οἶμον πρόεισιν [Loxon de oimon proeisin], It advances by an oblique path. And Nicander, comparing it with the cerastes in this very respect: [III, 209] Δοχμὰ δ᾽ ἐπισκάζει ὀλίγον δέμας, οἷα κεράστης· [Dochma d’ episkazei oligon demas, hoia kerastēs] It limps, bending its short body sideways, like the cerastes.

The cause lies in the vertebrae of the back, which are not bony, as in the rest, but cartilaginous, and so flexible in either direction that there can be no steadiness in their movement. To this point are these words of Lucan:
— — and the cerastes, wandering with twisting spine.
Accordingly Isidore states that the cerastes is so sinuous that it seems to have no spine. And Festus Avienus in the Description of the World:
Thus the long coils of the poisonous cerastes bend themselves of their own accord beneath their supple body.

But the poets trace the cause to Helen, who broke the spines of the kindred serpents, the cerastes and the haemorrhous, so as to make an offering to the shade of Canopus, her pilot, who had been killed in Egypt by the bite of a cerastes (or haemorrhous). Nicander, after seasoning this little tale with poetic wit, closes it with this epiphonema:

Ἔξοθεν αἱμοῤῥόοι, σκολιοπλανέες τε κεράσται, Οἷοι χωλεύουσι· — — — — [Exothen haimorrhooi, skolioplanees te kerastai, Hoioi chōleuousi] From then on the haemorrhous, and the cerastes, go lame, it is said, ploughing a crooked path. — — —

Similar things may be read in Conon, Hist. 8, and in Aelian, book 15, chapter 13. In these it should be noted above all that Nicander says that the haemorrhous and the cerastes, on account of their crooked gait, are the only serpents that χωλεύειν [chōleuein] and ἐπισκάζειν [episkazein], that is, limp. For from this the origin of the Hebrew name is evident. In Hebrew, namely among the masters, שפף saphaph is to limp, and שפוף saphuph is lame. Boderianus cites both in this sense from the book Beresith Rabba. The Talmudists too use שפי sephi and שפיפן sephiphon for lame, yet with this difference: they call שפי one who limps on one foot, and שפיפן one who limps on both feet, in Greek in one word ἀμφιγυήεις [amphigyēeis], which is the epithet of Vulcan in Homer and Hesiod. Hence in the tractate Sota, p. 10a: אמר ר׳ יוחנן בלעם חיגר ברגלו אחת שנאמר וילך שפי שמשון חיגר בשתי רגליו היה שנאמר שפיפן עלי ארח, R. Iochanan said: Balaam was lame in one foot, since it is said of him Num. XXIII, 3, "And he went שפי, lame." But Samson was lame in both feet; hence it is said of him Gen. XLIX, 17, "Sephiphon upon the path." These things, though utterly absurd, nevertheless teach what we want: namely, that the name שפיפון, in the opinion of the Hebrews, was formed from limping. So the sephiphon is a lame serpent, and there are none such, as far as I know, except the cerastes and the haemorrhous. It is therefore very probable that both are signified by this name.

[III, 210] As for Samson: since he was not only a Danite but also the most illustrious of the Danites, [col. 420] all the Hebrews refer to him what is said here. This has already been shown for the Talmudists. And the Jerusalem paraphrase says in so many words: והוא שמשון בר מנוח, He is Samson, son of Manoah. Jonathan and Onkelos too, though they do not name him, nevertheless clearly point to him, especially the former, whose words are: There shall be a man who will be chosen, and he will arise from the house of Dan. The fear of him shall fall upon the peoples, and he shall mightily smite the Philistines. Like a basilisk he shall lurk by the way, and like an asp he shall lie in wait by the path. He shall kill the mighty in the camp of the Philistines, horsemen together with foot soldiers; he shall hamstring horses and chariots (that is, the horses of the chariots, by the figure ἓν διὰ δυοῖν [hen dia dyoin]) and throw their riders backward. Why this is said of Samson is not clear enough, since the Sacred Writers nowhere relate that he had to do with the horsemen or chariots of the Philistines. Nor indeed is it necessary to refer to Samson alone what is said of the whole tribe, or to imagine here broken squadrons of horsemen. For the Danites are compared with the cerastes, which lurks in the way and bites the heels of horses, for no other reason than that they conducted their affairs by cunning rather than by open warfare. Of this we have an example in Iud. XVIII, 27., where the Danites attack the unsuspecting people of Laish. This is permitted in a just war. Brasidas in Thucydides, book 5: Τὰ κλέμματα ταῦτα καλλίστην δόξαν ἔχει, ἃ τὸν πολέμιον μάλιστ᾽ ἄν τις ἀπατήσας, τοὺς φίλους μέγιστ᾽ ἂν ὠφελήσειεν· [Ta klemmata tauta kallistēn doxan echei, ha ton polemion malist' an tis apatēsas, tous philous megist' an ōphelēseien] These stratagems of war win the finest glory, by which one, most deceiving the enemy, most helps one's friends. And Coroebus in book 2 of the Aeneid:
Let us exchange shields, and fit the insignia of the Greeks to ourselves. Trickery or valour, who would ask in an enemy?
And Corvinus in Silius, book 5:
War must be waged by cunning: lighter is the praise won by the avenging right hand.

This is how I prefer to read it, rather than the common reading indice dextra or in duce dextra. Accordingly Vegetius, De arte militari book 3, chapter 9, praises commanders who attempt battle, in which the danger is shared, not in open combat but always from concealment, so that, with their own forces as far as possible intact, they may surely destroy the enemy, or at least terrify them. And among our own writers Augustine, on Joshua, chapter 10: When he has undertaken a just war (the just man), whether he conquers in open battle or by ambush makes no difference to justice. Yet certain distinctions must be drawn here; since they do not belong to this place, they are to be sought from the illustrious Grotius, De jure belli book 3, chapter 1, section 6, etc.

It is surprising that some of the ancients refer these same words of Jacob both to Samson, with the Jews, and to the Antichrist, as though both were signified by the snake and the cerastes that lies in wait on the path. For Samson, a type of Christ and the deliverer of the church, cannot be described in the same words as the Antichrist, the enemy of Christ [III, 211] and the subverter of the church. Moreover, this interpretation is most strongly contradicted by the fact that in the Greek and Latin versions, which these doctors used, Jacob's words are framed as a wish: Γενηθήτω Δὰν ὄφις ἐφ᾽ ὁδοῦ [Genēthētō Dan ophis eph᾽ hodou], Let Dan be a snake on the path. For it is not plausible that Jacob wished the Antichrist to arise from his own stock. Rightly, therefore, does Bellarmine say on this passage, De Romano pontifice book 3, chapter 12: Jacob certainly seems to be blessing his son when he says this, and therefore to be foretelling not evil but good.

notes.text: Vincent, and the author of De nat. rerum.

The Arabs' معرن [mʿrn] or مقرن [muqarran], i.e. horned, is without doubt the Coluber cornutus of HASSELQUIST (Travels p. 241 and 365), who described this serpent accurately. I shall set down what is most to the point: "Two tentacles (horns?), one on each side, at the sides of the crown, on the upper margin of the orbit of the eye, erect, slightly arched on the rear side and slightly channelled on the same side, somewhat hard, clothed with a tough membrane, surrounded at the base by very small scales set erect in a single row, short, half the length of the orbits of the eyes." Compare also J. D. Michaelis, Notes on the vernacular version of the Bible, on Genes. XLIX, 17. and on Numer. XXI, 6., to which passage he also added a picture of the cerastes, after the drawing that J. ELLIS inserted in the Acts of the Royal Society of London (the philosophical Transactions), December 1766. Michaelis, however, wrongly thinks that the horned snake, the cerastes of the ancients, is the same as the basilisk of the ancients, which seems rather to be the coronella, and is called by the Arabs ملكة [malika], regulus; see our note 5 on Chapter X.

Observations, book 2, ch. 55, p. 122, Paris ed. 1555, of which Paulus gave an epitome in der Sammlung der merkwürdigsten Reisen in den Orient, vol. 1 p. 206. Nor will one regret comparing what a certain learned man, expert in natural history, remarks on this passage of BELON's Observatt. in the Notes appended to the second Part of Paulus's Collection, p. 258. Bruce too has much on the horned cerastes in his Travels vol. 5, p. 200 ff., German trans., and also added a picture of it at Plate 41.
